newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Post-vote tensions rise in Nicaragua.
newsitem.headline: Post-vote tensions rise in Nicaragua.

text.p: Nicaraguans said they were bracing for possible violence on Tuesday as the dispute over results from Nicaragua's presidential elections spilled over into the key race for mayor of Managua.
Tensions soared late on Monday when the two leading mayoral candidates each claimed victory, leading police to ban public demonstrations for fear of bloodshed.

Left-wing Sandinista firebrand Carlos Guadamuz, director of Sandinista-owned Radio Ya, announced that he had won the vote for Managua mayor based on a recount of the votes by his party, which complained the original count was riddled with "serious irregularities."
The preliminary count by election officials showed Guadamuz trailing by six points to Roberto Cedeno of the right-wing Liberal Alliance.
The Sandinista recount, not acknowledged by election authorities, reversed the result, giving Guadamuz a 30 to 28 percent lead over Cedeno, who maintains he is the winner.

The dispute shadows that of the presidential race, in which Liberal Alliance candidate Arnoldo Aleman, the fiercely anti-Sandinista former mayor of Managua, held a 49 to 38 percent lead over former President Daniel Ortega in the preliminary vote count.

But Ortega, who headed the 1979-1990 Sandinista government, has refused to concede defeat, saying the count is invalid and that he will wait for the final results of the Supreme Electoral Council's review of the voting acts.
The mayoral and presidential candidates of the two major parties have deep ties.

Ortega and Guadamuz formed an unshakable friendship after spending seven years together (1967-1974) in prison as Sandinista guerrillas conspiring against the former military dictatorship of Anastasio Somoza.
Cedeno was Aleman's hand-picked successor as mayor of Managua after Aleman stepped down in order to run for president.
In an address on his top-rated, sensationalistic radio station, Guadamuz called on his Sandinista supporters to defend his victory to the "ultimate consequences."

Caller after caller to Radio Ya said the left-wing Sandinistas were being robbed both of the mayor's chair and the presidency by election fraud perpetrated by the Liberals, and threatened popular insurrection.
"The Liberal Somocistas (supporters of the former dictator Somoza) are trying to rob us again, but we will defend our victory with arms if we have to," said caller Andrea Romero.
As hundreds of Guadamuz supporters gathered around Radio Ya headquarters to celebrate his self-proclaimed victory, National Police called for calm and banned demonstrations.

"We are worried by the intense climate of instability being created by the announcers of Radio Ya, who are practically calling for subversion against the authorities," said Cedeno, who continued to affirm his lead in vote.
Meanwhile right-wing Radio Corporacion fiercely defended Cedeno's victory, darkly warning of impending conflict if the Sandinista demands continued.

The rapidly escalating tensions underscored the lingering left-right polarisation that haunts Nicaragua almost seven years after its civil war between right-wing Contra rebels and the Marxist Sandinista government ended.

Nicaragua's top election official, Rosa Marina Zelaya, called on the two parties to put off proclaiming victory before the official results were in. "The CSE has not declared any winners so far in this election, much less in Managua, which has turned into one of the most conflictive departments in the revision process," Zelaya said.
The allegations of irregularities and fraud have sullied what was to have been a landmark step in Nicaragua's moves toward democracy after years of dictatorship and civil war.
The CSE said provisional results will be in by week's end.
